sentences: Monet painted the harbor of his hometown, Le Havre, as the sun rose.
Cranes and ships dissolve into mist; only the orange sun and its reflection on the water stand out sharp and clear.
In 1872 Monet stayed in Le Havre and painted the port several times.
This view looks southeast over the harbor from his hotel window, and according to the museum he finished it in just a few hours.
Look first at the upper part of the painted sky.
Streaks of orange and pink sweep across it at an angle, laid down very fast.
They seem to catch the brief moment when the dawn clouds first begin to colour.
On the left, the faint grey-blue shapes are the harbor cranes, masts and chimneys, melting into the mist.
Smoke rises among them, and Monet deliberately leaves every outline soft and unfinished.
Now let's look closely at the real star of the picture, the sun.
Curiously, the orange sun has almost exactly the same brightness as the grey-blue sky around it.
In a black-and-white photo the sun nearly vanishes altogether.
A Harvard neuroscientist explains that our brains handle luminance and colour separately.
With no difference in luminance to hold it in place, the sun seems to shimmer on the canvas.
Below the sun, its reflection runs down across the water.
Monet simply dabbed on orange paint in quick, short strokes, and with only those few touches the rippling light comes vividly alive.
In the small boat in front, a figure stands at the oar, and two more boats float in the haze behind.
According to the museum, these boats, the sun and its reflection were the last things Monet added.
At the lower left are Monet's signature and the number 72.
An astronomer later calculated the sun's height and the tides, and dated the scene to about 7:35 in the morning on 13 November 1872.
Monet recalled that it could hardly pass as a view of Le Havre, so he said, put down Impression.
At an 1874 exhibition, a critic mocked the title and called the whole group Impressionists.
The insult stuck, and Impressionism became the name of the whole movement.
The painting was stolen in 1985 and recovered in 1990.
Today it hangs once again in the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris.
Not a finished picture but an impression of a passing moment of light: that was the beginning of a new art.
Narrow your eyes a little and look at the sun once more.
Is it really trembling?
